title: Other people's faults (244–255)
hook: others' faults are easy to see, our own hard; we winnow theirs like chaff and hide our own (Dhammapada 252)

segments.voice: Yesterday, mala: dross blown off one by one, little by little. Your line was little by little.

Hand someone a stranger's essay and a red pen, and the mistakes leap off the page: a clumsy sentence here, a missing word there. Hand them their own essay, and the same mistakes go invisible. Or listen to a friend describe her sister, every flaw laid out in perfect detail. Ask for her own three biggest flaws, and there's a long pause. A perfect view of other people, and a blind spot the size of a truck about ourselves. Chapter eighteen names it exactly.
screen: `A RED PEN ON SOMEONE ELSE'S ESSAY.` → `ON YOUR OWN ESSAY, NOTHING.` → `A BLIND SPOT THE SIZE OF A TRUCK.`

segments.voice: Verse two fifty-two, in Max Müller's translation: "The fault of others is easily perceived, but that of oneself is difficult to perceive; a man winnows his neighbour's faults like chaff, but his own fault he hides, as a cheat hides the bad die from the gambler." Two pictures in one verse. First, winnowing: at harvest, farmers tossed grain into the wind so the light chaff would blow away. Picture someone tossing another person's faults high into the air, scattering them across the whole village. Second, a cheat at dice, hiding the bad die so no one notices it. That's what we do with our own. The Pali word for fault here is vajja, something to be avoided, something blameworthy. The next verse warns what happens to the fault-finder. Verse two fifty-three: "If a man looks after the faults of others, and is always inclined to be offended, his own passions will grow". The irony is sharp. Constant judging doesn't make you better. It feeds the very things you're judging. Just before these lines, verse two fifty-one gives four more pictures: "There is no fire like passion, there is no shark like hatred, there is no snare like folly, there is no torrent like greed." Then the chapter closes with a reminder that a person isn't made holy by outward show, which is where tomorrow's chapter picks up. None of this says other people have no faults. It says the eye that sees theirs so clearly would do its best work turned around.
screen: `WINNOWING SOMEONE ELSE'S CHAFF.` · `THE CHEAT HIDES THE BAD DIE.` · `JUDGING FEEDS WHAT IT JUDGES.` · `NO SHARK LIKE HATRED.` · then, large: `EASY TO SEE OTHERS.`

segments.voice: Think of someone whose faults you know by heart, name one silently, and gently turn the same bright light around: is there any trace of it in you? Not to punish yourself, just to look, the way you'd check your own mirror; often there's a small echo, and if there isn't, look for the fault you'd least like anyone to see. When you've seen it, oh, there it is, set it down and let the breath be plain and open.
Vajja. A fault, something blameworthy: verse two fifty-two says others' faults are easy to see, while our own are hard to see; we winnow theirs like chaff and hide our own.
Your line: easy to see others. Hard to see ourselves. Day two hundred six, done.

howItsDone: Buddhist monastics regularly confess their own faults to one another, and teachers often cite verse 252 to turn attention from criticizing others to examining oneself.

original.note: Pali: a fault, something to be avoided — sudassaṃ vajjam aññesaṃ, others' faults are easy to see.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't be judgmental.
what it means: we see others' faults clearly and hide our own, and constant fault-finding only feeds our own passions.
what a scholar hears: verse 252 pairs two images: winnowing (opuṇāti) the chaff of others' faults and hiding one's own like a crooked gambler hides the losing throw.
recall: being satisfied with what you already have

chat.says: Why is it so easy to spot my brother's flaws but so hard to see my own?
options: The verse names it: others' faults are easy to see, our own hard. We winnow theirs, hide ours.
Because his flaws are bigger; the verse says we see most clearly whoever has more faults.
The verse says looking hard at others' faults is how you get rid of your own.
chat.meaning: Verse 252: others' faults are easily seen, our own hardly. We winnow a neighbor's faults like chaff, and hide our own like a cheat hides a bad die.
